ECEA 5306 Linux Kernel Programming and Introduction to Yocto Project

Instructor: Dan Walkes

Course Description

This course provides an introduction to Kernel programming for the Linux operating system, and the development of Linux kernel drivers for Embedded devices. The Yocto build system is introduced, which students use to build their own custom Embedded Linux system through programming assignments.

It is the student’s responsibility to monitor these deadlines. Coursera and CU Boulder are not responsible for notifying the students of these deadlines. You can drop or withdraw from a course via Your Programs & Enrollment Card via BuffPortal.

Assignment 6 Part 1: Native Socket Server Threading Support

Note that this assignment will require changes to your assignment 3 repository (referred to as your aesd-assignments repository below), and will also require some additional code for this assignment.

GitHub Repository Links

Please find the link to create your repository for this assignment in the "GitHub Repo Creation Links" section under course resources. You may find course resources on the left side pane of your module view.

Setting up your Assignment Repository

Execute the following instructions in your aesd-assignments assignment 3 repository local repository folder:

  1. git fetch assignments-base

This step assumes you’ve already created the remote using git remote add assignments-base git@github.com:cu-ecen-aeld/aesd-assignments.git in assignment 2.  If you started from a new repo you’ll need to re-run the git remote-add step before attempting to fetch.

  1. git merge assignments-base/assignment6

  2. git submodule update --init --recursive

Also make sure your aesd-assignments repository origin still points to your assignment 3 repository using git remote get-url origin

The following links are external and will open in a new tab.

Suggested Reading:

  1. Associated video content

  2. Linked List Documentation:

a. https://blog.taborkelly.net/programming/c/2016/01/09/sys-queue-example.html

b. https://web.archive.org/web/20260429190109/http://cslibrary.stanford.edu/103/LinkedListBasics.pdf

Implementation:

Continuation of Assignment 5:

  1. Modify your socket based program to accept multiple simultaneous connections, with each connection spawning a new thread to handle the connection.

    1. Writes to /var/tmp/aesdsocketdata should be synchronized between threads using a mutex, to ensure data written by synchronous connections is not intermixed, and not relying on any file system synchronization.

      1. For instance, if one connection writes “12345678” and another connection writes “abcdefg” it should not be possible for the resulting /var/tmp/aesdsocketdata file to contain a mix like “123abcdefg456”, the content should always be “12345678”, followed by “abcdefg”. However for any simultaneous connections, it's acceptable to allow packet writes to occur in any order in the socketdata file.

    2. The thread should exit when the connection is closed by the client or when an error occurs in the send or receive steps.

    3. Your program should continue to gracefully exit when SIGTERM/SIGINT is received, after requesting an exit from each thread and waiting for threads to complete execution.

    4. Use the singly linked list APIs discussed in the video (or your own implementation if you prefer) to manage threads.

      1. Use pthread_join() to join completed threads, do not use detached threads for this assignment.

  2. Modify your aesdsocket source code repository to:

    1. Append a timestamp in the form “timestamp:time” where time is specified by the RFC 2822 compliant strftime format, followed by newline (external link; opens in a new tab).  This string should be appended to the /var/tmp/aesdsocketdata file every 10 seconds, where the string includes the year, month, day, hour (in 24 hour format) minute and second representing the system wall clock time.

    2. Use appropriate locking to ensure the timestamp is written atomically with respect to socket data Hint:  Think where should the timer be initialized. Should it be initialized in parent or child?

  3. Use the updated sockettest.sh script (in the assignment-autotest/test/assignment6 subdirectory) . You can run this manually outside the `./full-test.sh` script by:

    1. Starting your aesdsocket application

    2. Executing the sockettest.sh script from the assignment-autotest subdirectory.

    3. Stopping your aesdsocket application.

  4. The `./full-test.sh` script in your aesd-assignments repository should now complete successfully.

  5. Tag the assignment with “assignment-<assignment number>-complete” once the final commit is pushed onto your repository. The instructions to add a tag can be found here (external link; opens in a new tab)

Validation:

  1. The automated test environment should pass when running against your assignment implementation.

2. You should not have any memory leaks or errors identified when running valgrind.

Troubleshooting:

Blocked Multithreaded Sockets with valgrind

You may notice that your multithread socket test fails and your multithreaded sockets threads aren't actually running. You may notice that if you add --fair-sched=yes to the valgrind command line arguments the test succeeds.

This typically happens because you are using polling instead of non-blocking calls for accept and have a tight while(1) loop or similar in the main thread which is waiting for threads to complete. In this case with the added valgrind overhead the socket threads may not run at all.

  • One solution is to follow the assignment recommendations to block on accept in the main loop and free completed threads only after starting the next thread.

  • An alternative solution is to add a delay in the non-blocking accept implementation and ideally to block on an fd you can signal when the thread exits or something similar.

GitHub Repository Links

Implementation:

Setup Github Actions:

For this and later yocto assignments you need to setup your SSH key as a repository secret.

Yocto Installation

  1. Install essential build packages on your build host as described in the “Build Host Packages” section of the yocto quick start guide.

  2. Add yocto poky as a git submodule in the root of your project repository.

    1. Use https://git.yoctoproject.org/poky as the source (see the clone reference at https://git.yoctoproject.org/poky/)

    2. Be sure to git add from the root of your project repository and git commit to save the appropriate commit hash for the buildroot directory before running ./build.sh

    3. Use the branch kirkstone

  3. Update the recipe “aesd-assignments” in the meta-aesd/recipes-aesd folder of your project as discussed in class. This recipe should build your assignment 6 aesdsocket source using the git repository with appropriate commit specified via SRCREV and install associated files in the rootfs of the system.

    1. Remember to add your start script as well using the instructions discussed in lecture videos.

  4. Add your package to core-image-aesd as described in lecture videos.

  5. Use the build.sh script to build your combined image

  6. Use the runqemu.sh script in the root folder which:

    1. Runs source oe-init-build-env from the poky directory to setup your yocto build environment.

    2. Uses runqemu nographic plus appropriate arguments to start QEMU with host port 9000 forwarded to your QEMU instance using slirp.

  7. If not already present, add ssh support to your image using CORE_IMAGE_EXTRA_INSTALL += " openssh" in your core-image-aesd.bb file.

  8. Verify your socket is started automatically when starting qemu on the target. Verify your socket test scripts used for part 1 of your assignment work as expected when running against the qemu target, as they did with the assignment 5 buildroot implementation.

    1. The `./full-test.sh` script in your yocto repository should now complete successfully.  Ensure you have installed sshpass with `sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y sshpass` as this is required for the test script.

  9. Tag the assignment with “assignment-<assignment number>-complete” once the final commit is pushed onto the respective repositories. The instructions to add a tag can be found here

Validation:

  1. You should be able to clone your final yocto assignment repository to a new directory, run ./build.sh to build the system image and ./runqemu.sh to start the image.

  2. When the QEMU image is started, it should pass port 9000 from the host into the guest image, the aesdsocket utility should be running in daemon mode, and all functionality should match the implementation section.

This means the logic we have here to remove timestamps from the output file is failing, because the socket output file is being treated as a binary file instead of a text file (external link; opens in a new tab). The reason the output file is treated as a binary file is typically because there are non-printable ASCII characters in the file. There may be non printable ASCII characters in the file for a variety of reason but the most common is probably exceeding array bounds on strings which are missing null termination characters. Look at the output file with a hex editor, find where the binary content is included, and fix your code to ensure you aren't writing anything other than the ASCII string content sent over the socket into your socket file.

  2. Use the cleanall task in bitbake (documentation here (external link; opens in a new tab)) to recover from failures of recipe builds. This will help you clean build a specific recipe. For instance, sometimes recipes fail to build if your build machine crashed when building due to out of disk space or out of memory conditions.   2. Add INHERIT += "rm_work" in your build.conf as referenced here, either by manually editing the build/conf/local.conf file or editing the build script to add this to the file.

Use the previous kernel set as BR2_LINUX_KERNEL_CUSTOM_CONFIG_FILE in your aesd_qemu_defconfig file as the initial content of this file by copying from the buildroot directory to your base_external path specified in the kernel submenu. You can do this with command cp buildroot/board/qemu/aarch64-virt/linux.config base_external/configs/linux.config

  2. make linux-menuconfig from buildroot directory

  3. Enable the following options:

    1. kernel hacking -> kernel debugging

    2. kernel hacking -> memory debugging -> kernel memory leak detector

    3. kernel hacking -> memory debugging -> Simple test for the kernel memory leak detector (This option would install a module which would have memory leaks.)

    4. kernel hacking -> memory debugging -> Maximum kmemleak early log entries - set to 4096 (see https://stackoverflow.com/questions/55764173/kernel-memory-leak-detector)

    5. kernel hacking->Sample Kernel Code

  4. Save the configuration using save-config.sh, build using build.sh and run qemu.

  5. Build and boot up the resulting image in qemu. If the debugfs isn't already mounted, mount with:

    1. mount -t debugfs nodev /sys/kernel/debug/

  6. Enter the following commands on terminal to check if the kernel memory leak detector has been properly installed and is detecting memory leaks.  This loads a module that deliberately leaks memory called “kmemleak-test”

    1. echo clear > /sys/kernel/debug/kmemleak

    2. modprobe kmemleak-test

    3. echo scan > /sys/kernel/debug/kmemleak

    4. cat /sys/kernel/debug/kmemleak

      1. You should see memory leaks identified, which proves your leak test kernel config is working.

    5. rmmod kmemleak-test

  7. Reboot and repeat steps 4 and 5 using your module instead of kmemleak-test, removing and adding your module after clearing any existing memory leaks.

    1. You should see no memory leaks identified by the scan step for /sys/kernel/debug/kmemleak when loading your module.

Validation:

  1. Your driver should pass the drivertest.sh script provided with the assignment

  2. Your qemu instance should pass the sockettest script, this time writing and reading from only the /dev/aesdchar device instead of /var/tmp/aesdsocketdata.

  3. Your implementation should not crash or have memory leaks.

  4. Your implementation should use proper locking methods to ensure safe access from multiple threads or processes.

  5. Your project should contain build.sh, clean.sh, and runqemu.sh scripts which function as specified in previous assignments, and can successfully clean, build, and run your project without user interaction for automated build testing.

Submission:

  1. Your submission repository should contain a working buildroot or yocto implementation.

  2. Your buildroot or yocto implementation should reference a commit in your assignments 3 and later repository containing the code added for this assignment.

Troubleshooting

  1. Attempts to run full-test on qemu fails with rmmod: Can't unload aesdchar resource temporarily unavailable

    1. If your test script fails during the driver test step due to failure to unload your driver, please ensure you are not opening the file descriptor for your driver endpoint from aesdsocket until it is accessed.

    2. If your sockettest application opens the file descriptor at startup and does not close it, this will prevent the script from successfully testing your driver in isolation by unloading/reloading it. Please modify your aesdsocket application to only open the file descriptor for your /dev/aesdchar device when reading/writing and otherwise close it when not in use or before initial use

Assignment 9: Advanced Char Driver Operations

GitHub Repository Links

Please find the link to create your repository for this assignment in the "GitHub Repo Creation Links" section under course resources. You may find course resources on the left side pane of your module view.

Suggested Reading:

  1. Linux Device Drivers book chapters 3-6

GitHub Repository Start Instructions

You will start with an empty project submission repository, and fill it with the content of your assignment 8 local repository using these commands on your local buildroot-assignments repository or yocto assignments repository

  1. git remote rename origin assignment-8-remote

  2. git remote add origin <your github classroom submission repo created with the link above>

  3. git push origin main

Repository Setup:

Note: The following links are external and will open in a new tab.

Implementation:

  1. Pick either the Buildroot or Yocto implementation from Assignment 8 (which are located in assignment 5 or 6 repositories respectively) to use as the basis for your assignment and push to your submission repository.  You can use either Buildroot or Yocto for this assignment.  For a buildroot implementation, use

    1. git fetch buildroot-assignments-base

      1. This step assumes you’ve already created the remote using git remote add buildroot-assignments-base  https://github.com/cu-ecen-aeld/buildroot-assignments-base.git in assignment 5.  If you started from a new repo you’ll need to re-run the git remote-add step before attempting to fetch.

    2. git merge -X theirs buildroot-assignments-base/assignment9

      1. If you notice merge conflicts during the merge step with the assignment-autotest submodule, use:

        1. git checkout --theirs aesd-assignments/assignment9 -- assignment-autotest

        2. git commit

      2. git submodule update --init --recursive

  2. Using your assignment 3 repository, complete the following steps to pull in content from the aesd-assignments repository assignment-8 branch

    a.  git fetch assignments-base

    This step assumes you’ve already created the remote using git remote add assignments-base git@github.com:cu-ecen-aeld/aesd-assignments.git in the previous assignment.  If you started from a new repo you’ll need to re-run the git remote add step before attempting to fetch.

    b. git merge -X theirs assignments-base/assignment9

    i. If you notice merge conflicts during the merge step with the assignment-autotest submodule, use:

    1. git checkout --theirs git assignments-base/assignment9 -- assignment-autotest

    2. git commit

    c. git submodule update --init --recursive

  3. Update your “aesd-char-driver” implementation in your assignment 3 and later repository to add the following features:

    1. Add custom seek support to your driver using the llseek file_operations function.  Your seek implementation should:

      1. Support all positional types (SEEK_SET, SEEK_CUR, and SEEK_END) and update the file position accordingly.

        1. For instance, if your driver is storing writes of 5, 7, and 9 bytes each, an file position of 0-5 would represent a byte within the first write, a file position of 6-13 would represent a byte within the second write, and a file position of 14 through 23 would a byte within represent the 3rd write.

    For instance: Consider the content in the table below as handled by your driver, where each string ends with a newline character. An offset of 15 would set the pointer to the second byte of the word “Singapore”, byte "i"

    Grass

    Sentosa

    Singapore

  4. Add ioctl command support for AESDCHAR_IOCSEEKTO as defined in aesd_ioctl.h which is passed a  buffer from user space containing two 4 byte values. Use unlocked_ioctl to implement your ioctl command

    1. The first value represents the command to seek into, based on a zero referenced number of commands currently stored by the driver in the command circular buffer. The command reference is relative to the number of commands currently stored in your circular buffer. You will need to translate into the appropriate offset within your circular buffer based on the current location of the output index.

      1. For instance, in the example above a value of 0 refers to the command “Grass\n”

    2. The second value represents the zero referenced offset within this command to seek into.  All offsets are specified relative to the start of the request.

      1. For instance, if the offset was 2 in the command “Grass”, the seek location should be the letter “a”

    3. The two parameters above will seek to the appropriate place and update the file pointer as described in the seek support details within the previous step.

    4. If the two parameters are out of range of the number of write commands/command length, the ioctl cmd should return -EINVAL

  5. Add special handling for socket write commands to your aesdsocket server application

    1. When the string sent over the socket equals AESDCHAR_IOCSEEKTO:X,Y where X and Y are unsigned decimal integer values, the X should be considered the write command to seek into and the Y should be considered the offset within the write command.

    2. These values should be sent to your driver using the AESDCHAR_IOCSEEKTO ioctl described earlier.  The ioctl command should be performed before any additional writes to your aesdchar device.

    3. Do not write this string command into the aesdchar device as you do with other strings sent to the socket.

    4. Send the content of the aesdchar device back over the socket, as you do with any other string received over the socket interface. We will use this to test the seek command.

    5. Ensure the read of the file and return over the socket uses the same (not closed and re-opened) file descriptor used to send the ioctl, to ensure your file offset is honored for the read command.

6. Tag the assignment with assignment-<assignment number>-complete once the final commit is pushed onto the respective repositories. The instructions to add a tag can be found here

Validation:

  1. Your qemu instance should pass the modified sockettest script which includes tests for ioctl command sends.

  2. Your implementation should not crash or have memory leaks.

  3. Your implementation should use proper locking methods to ensure safe access from multiple threads or processes.

  4. Your driver should include custom seek and ioctl commands as described in the implementation section.

    1. When behavior in a specific scenario is not specified in your driver requirements, you should use any best practices mentioned in the Linux Device Drivers book.

  5. Your aesdsocket application should include support for custom socket commands as described in the implementation section.

  6. Your implementation should pass when running with the full-test.sh script

Troubleshooting:

1. Attempts to issue ioctl returns "Inappropriate ioctl for device".

  • Ensure your driver is connected to the /dev/aesdchar endpoint through mknod. Ensure you aren't deleting or attempting to create the /dev/aesdchar endpoint within your aesdsocket application.

  • Ensure you've implemented the unlocked_ioctl call in your driver (implementing compat_ioctl is not sufficient).

  • Double check your buildroot submodule and linux kernel version. If you are using a 6.x kernel version through a later buildroot submodule revision than the branch currently recommended for assignments you must define compat_ioctl. Using a definition .compat_ioctl = compat_ptr_ioctl should resolve the issue, or you can move back to the buildroot branch recommended in assignment 5.

2. Attempts to run full-test on qemu fails with rmmod: Can't unload aesdchar resource temporarily unavailable

  • If your test script fails during the driver test step due to failure to unload your driver, please ensure you are not opening the file descriptor for your driver endpoint from aesdsocket until it is accessed.

  • If your sockettest application opens the file descriptor at startup and does not close it, this will prevent the script from successfully testing your driver in isolation by unloading/reloading it. Please modify your aesdsocket application to only open the file descriptor for your /dev/aesdchar device when reading/writing and otherwise close it when not in use or before initial use

The course final examination is similar in format to the homework quiz assignments, with the following important differences.

Permitted Exam Materials

You may use the following when taking the exam:

  • A notes sheet of paper, front and back, with 11pt or larger font if not hand-written. These notes must be your own and not copied from another student.

  • An electronic copy of your notes sheet, if you prefer this to a physical paper.

  • One URL containing your notes (for example, a Google Drive link or similar online editor).

  • Pens, pencils, blank paper as desired.

Prohibited Exam Materials

You may not use the following when taking the exam:

  • Course textbooks.

  • Lecture slides and lecture content.

  • AI Tools.

You may drop or withdraw from this course at any time before accessing the final exam. Once you begin the exam, you will be assigned a course grade based on the announced grading formula, and this grade will appear on your university transcript after the eight-week session concludes. After the final exam has ended, you may continue submitting homework assignments until the conclusion of the eight-week session.

How ME-ECE Uses Virtual/Remote Proctoring

Most for-credit MS-ECE courses feature a proctored experience at the end of the course. This is generally an exam, but may also be a project-based experience. The University of Colorado Boulder takes academic integrity seriously, and is committed to ensuring that your MS-ECE degree accurately represents your competency and retains its value in the marketplace. Protecting the integrity of the course exams is part of this process.

The stakes of the proctored experiences in MS-ECE courses are high. When you gain access to these protected items on the Coursera platform, you are no longer eligible for a tuition refund if you decide to drop the course, and you are no longer eligible for a course withdrawal. Accessing the protected examination means that you will only be eligible for an earned grade based on performance.

What is ProctorU?

ProctorU is a platform that is partnered with your institution to help you take an exam online while ensuring academic integrity is upheld. Using this platform allows you the convenience of testing from home 24/7, 365 days a year. 

How it Works

  1. Create a ProctorU account.

    1. Click here to get started.

  2. Download the Guardian Secure Browser.

  3. Schedule at least 72 hours in advance of the date/time you want to take your exam.

    1. Login and click the “Schedule New Session” button.

    2. Confirm your institution, term, and exam name, then click “Search Sessions.”

    3. Use the calendar and clock features on the left to select your desired testing date and time.

    4. Click here to log in to your ProctorU account and test your equipment.

  4. Click here to log in to your ProctorU account and test your equipment.

    1. 5 Steps for Student Guide

Important Reminders

Note: Last Day and Time to Schedule ProctorU Exam will always be 3 days prior to the end of the session. It will always fall on a Tuesday, 4:50pm MT.

We strongly recommend that you do not start the proctored exam process until you are ready to take the exam and complete the course. Find more details about the relationship between proctored experiences and course drops/refunds in the MS-ECE on Coursera Student Handbook.

  • You must schedule your exam at least 72 hours in advance of your desired day and time. For example, if the exam availability window closes at 4:50 pm on a Friday, the last time you could schedule an exam would be that Tuesday at 4:50 pm.

  • To secure your desired exam session time, log into ProctorU and schedule your session as soon as you know your desired exams session date and time.

  • A reflective surface handy
